steps.observation: You have 30 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three days when Elias woke to the sound of footsteps on the stair.

No supply boat, no storms, no one radioing in. Just the sea, the gulls, and the steady blink of the lamp that he had trimmed and polished twice a day for thirty-seven years. The lighthouse stood alone on a black tooth of rock twelve miles off the coast. No one came without warning.

The footsteps were slow, deliberate, working their way up through the tower’s stone throat. Elias put down his mug, listening. Old joints, he thought. Whoever it is is old, or tired, or both.

When the knock came, it was polite—three soft raps on the iron hatch that led to the lantern room.

Elias opened it to find a boy of perhaps sixteen, soaked to the bone, hair plastered to his forehead. No boat at the landing below, no sound of oars.

“You’re not supposed to be here,” Elias said.

The boy smiled, the sort of smile that forgot itself halfway through. “I got turned around in the fog.”

“There is no fog.”

The boy glanced past him to the lens, where the lamp burned like a patient star. “There was,” he said quietly. “I saw your light.”

Elias let him in. He’d long since learned that the sea didn’t always deliver things that made sense.

They sat across from one another in the small circular room as the lantern turned with its measured grace, glass prisms throwing slow, revolving specters across the walls. Elias brewed tea. The boy held the mug with both hands, more for comfort than heat.

“What’s your name?” Elias asked.

“Jacob.”

Elias tried the name on his tongue. It tasted familiar. “You shouldn’t be out here alone, Jacob.”

“I wasn’t,” the boy said. “My father was with me. There was a storm. We couldn’t see the shore. He said to watch for the lighthouse.” Jacob raised his eyes. “But the light was gone. So I followed the sound instead.”

“The horn,” Elias said. “But the foghorn’s been out of order.”

Jacob looked puzzled. “No, I heard it. Low and far away, like… like someone calling my name through a shell.” He swallowed. “The boat tipped. I went under. When I came up, I just… walked toward the sound. And then there were stairs, and a door, and you.”

Elias’s hand tightened around his own mug. There was something in the boy’s blue eyes, a shape he had not seen in decades except in the mirror. He knew now why the name was familiar.

“My son was named Jacob,” he said.

The boy’s face changed almost imperceptibly, as if a curtain shifted behind his eyes. “I know,” he answered.

The lantern hummed over them, its motor an old, contented animal. Outside, the ocean rolled and breathed, vast and indifferent.

“I remember this room,” Jacob said. His voice had lost its tremor. “The first time I came up here, you wouldn’t let me touch the lamp. You said if the light went out, ships would die. So I promised I’d never fail it.”

Elias stared. On his wall, in a rusted frame, was an old photograph: a woman laughing, a man younger by half and so certain of himself, and between them a small boy squinting into the sun, hair blown wild by the wind. Jacob at eight, before the fever took him in town, far from the sea and beyond the reach of any lighthouse.

“You died,” Elias whispered. “You never came back here.”

Jacob looked at him with a softness that hurt. “I tried.”

The old keeper’s throat constricted. All the lonely years, all the nights counted not by sleep but by rotations of the beam—suddenly they had weight and shape.

“Why now?” Elias asked. “After all this time?”

“The horn called me,” Jacob said simply. “You’ve been blowing it a long time, even if you didn’t hear it yourself.”

Elias thought of the habits you fall into alone: the way he spoke aloud when no one was there, the way he tapped rhythms on the rail, the way he watched every storm as if something might emerge from it at last. A private, wordless summons.

“The sea brought you?” Elias said.

“The sea returns what it owes,” Jacob replied. “But it asks a price.”

Elias looked at the lamp, its flame steady as a held breath. “My light,” he said.

Jacob followed his gaze. “They’ve built another lighthouse on the headland. Bigger, electric, seen for miles. Yours is a memory, father. Ships don’t look for you anymore.”

The words were not cruel. That made them worse.

“If I leave,” Elias murmured, “this rock goes dark.”

“If you stay,” Jacob said, “you go dark. Alone. Quietly.”

The iron and glass room suddenly felt very small. Outside, the sea stretched in every direction, endless and unknowable, yet every inch of it for miles had been his responsibility. His duty. His penance, perhaps.

“What happens to the light?” he asked.

Jacob set down his empty cup. The lamp’s reflection burned in his pupils. “It will shine as long as someone remembers it. You’ve done your part.”

Silence climbed the stairs between them. The old motor ticked. The lens turned. Far out, the ghost of a wave broke itself against an invisible reef.

“Will it hurt?” Elias asked.

Jacob shook his head. “You’ve been walking toward this staircase for years.”

Elias thought of the day he’d taken the posting. His wife gone to the city, his son buried under a stone with a ship carved into it. The world had seemed too wide, too bright, too crowded with ghosts. Here, on the rock, the ghosts had structure. Storms made sense. Lights had purpose.

“What if another ship needs me?” he whispered.

Jacob stood and offered his hand, palm as solid and warm as any living boy’s. “They’ll have their own beacons. You’ve spent your life saving strangers from rocks you could see. There is someone now, in another kind of fog, who needs you to come home.”

Elias saw, then, that the boy was not alone. Behind him, in the curved glass, a woman’s outline waited: hair tied back in the way she used to, one hand on the rail, the other outstretched in patient invitation.

Something in his chest unclenched.

He rose slowly, his joints complaining, and took Jacob’s hand. Together they turned toward the hatch. Each step down the spiral stair was lighter than the one before. The stone felt less like a prison, more like a body he was setting gently aside.

Halfway down, he paused and looked back. Through the open hatch, the lamp still burned, haloed in its glass, sending its steady breath of light out into the indifferent dark.

“Goodbye,” he said—not to the boy or the woman, but to the tower itself.

Below, at the waterline, there was no longer a landing, no boat, no ladder. Only a path of white foam, bright as a road in moonlight, reaching out across the black water. Jacob stepped onto it as if onto a pier, and the sea held him. Elias followed.

Behind him, the lighthouse watched a moment longer, then, very gently, its light began to fade—first from the glass, then from the stone, then from the memory of charts and logs and radio calls.

Out on the headland, the new electric beacon turned, its bright, hard beam skipping past the empty rock entirely. No ships were lost for lack of the old light.

On certain nights, though, when the fog is just right, sailors still hear a low horn far off the charts, and some say they see, for a heartbeat, the warm, impossible glow of a lamp lit by a man who has finally gone home.
